claims.sentence: Lung cancer is mostly divided into two groups, called non-small cell and small cell lung cancer.
claims.evidence: MedlinePlus: NSCLC 85 percent, SCLC remaining 15 percent

claims.sentence: Roy Castle says around 85 in every 100 people with lung cancer have a non-small cell type and about 15 in 100 have small cell lung cancer.
claims.evidence: Figures 85/15 carried by MedlinePlus; the Roy Castle page was not returned, so the attribution is unverified
claims.newSentence: MedlinePlus says non-small cell lung cancer accounts for 85 percent of lung cancer, and small cell lung cancer accounts for the remaining 15 percent.

claims.sentence: Adenocarcinoma is the most common kind of non-small cell cancer.
claims.evidence: Search text said adenocarcinoma is the most common type (unnamed page); undisputed textbook fact

claims.sentence: It grows more slowly than some other types, but it can spread early.
claims.evidence: Nothing retrieved for adenocarcinoma growth or early spread; only patent text on well-differentiated squamous growing slowly

claims.sentence: Squamous cell carcinoma starts in the cells that line the airways and is often caused by smoking.
claims.evidence: Only patent text; search itself noted no health-publisher text established the smoking link

claims.sentence: Large cell carcinoma is less common and tends to spread outside the lung at an earlier stage than other non-small cell types.
claims.evidence: Search explicitly found no source for early spread of large cell carcinoma

claims.sentence: Small cell lung cancer grows and spreads more quickly than the non-small cell types and is strongly linked with smoking.
claims.evidence: Only patent documents said SCLC grows rapidly and is almost always caused by smoking; no publisher page returned

claims.sentence: Because small cell cancer often spreads quite early, doctors generally treat it as if it has spread, whether or not a secondary cancer shows up.
claims.evidence: Only patent text; NHS says surgery is not usually used for SCLC because it has often already spread by diagnosis
claims.newSentence: It also says surgery is not usually used to treat small cell lung cancer, because the cancer has often already spread to other areas of the body by the time it is diagnosed.

claims.sentence: Knowing the type matters, because the NHS says treatment depends on the type of lung cancer and how far it has spread.
claims.evidence: NHS: treatment depends on size and location, type, whether spread, genetic changes, general health
claims.newSentence: The NHS says treatment depends on the size of the cancer and where it is, the type of lung cancer, whether it has spread, whether it has certain genetic changes and the person's general health.

claims.sentence: Staging describes how far a cancer has grown and spread.
claims.evidence: Plain textbook definition; not needed

claims.sentence: Cancer Research UK says the TNM system is the most common way to stage lung cancer.
claims.evidence: CRUK: TNM stands for Tumour, Node, Metastasis; most common way to stage lung cancer

claims.sentence: The number system uses TNM to place lung cancers into stages 1 to 4.
claims.evidence: CRUK: number staging uses TNM, stages run 1 to 4

claims.sentence: Macmillan says doctors use the same staging system for non-small cell and small cell lung cancer.
claims.evidence: Not carried by retrieved Macmillan text (which described limited/extensive wording)

claims.sentence: Small cell lung cancer may also be described as limited or extensive stage.
claims.evidence: CRUK limited/extensive page returned

claims.sentence: Cancer Research UK calls this an older, simpler system that is becoming less common.
claims.evidence: CRUK: simpler and older system, used less often as more is learned about SCLC

claims.sentence: Limited stage means the cancer is within a single area on one side of the chest.
claims.evidence: Retrieved wording differs: Macmillan says cancer cells seen in one lung and nearby lymph nodes
claims.newSentence: Macmillan describes limited stage as cancer cells that can be seen in one lung and in nearby lymph nodes

claims.sentence: Extensive stage means it has spread beyond a single area that can be treated with radiotherapy.
claims.evidence: Retrieved wording differs: Macmillan says spread outside the lung, to the chest area or other parts of the body
claims.newSentence: extensive stage as cancer that has spread outside the lung, to the chest area or to other parts of the body.

claims.sentence: Cancer Research UK adds that extensive disease generally means stage 4 small cell lung cancer.
claims.evidence: Retrieval attributes stage IV with distant metastases to NCI, not CRUK
claims.newSentence: The National Cancer Institute defines extensive stage as TNM stage IV with distant metastases.

claims.sentence: Roy Castle says stage 4 lung cancer is not curable but it is treatable, and many people can live well with advanced cancer.
claims.evidence: Roy Castle stage 4 page text, verbatim. Flagged: contains 'not curable' (sourced, general, not individual advice)

claims.sentence: A chest X-ray is often one of the first tests when a GP has any concern about lung cancer.
claims.evidence: Search: chest X-ray is usually the first test, often cannot give a definitive diagnosis alone
claims.newSentence: A chest X-ray is usually the first test for lung cancer. It often cannot give a definitive diagnosis on its own.

claims.sentence: A CT scan is the main imaging step.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: CT is usually the next test after a chest X-ray
claims.newSentence: A CT scan is usually the next test.

claims.sentence: It helps show where the cancer is and whether it may have spread to other organs, and the person lies on a table that slides into the scanner.
claims.evidence: Not carried by retrieved text

claims.sentence: In a bronchoscopy, a thin scope is passed through the airways so doctors can look inside and take a tiny tissue sample, called a biopsy.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: doctor can look inside the airways and remove a small sample of cells (thin scope detail not retrieved)
claims.newSentence: a bronchoscopy lets the doctor look inside the airways and remove a small sample of cells.

claims.sentence: Sometimes a needle biopsy through the skin is used instead.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: CT-guided needle biopsy, thin hollow needle through the chest wall into the lung; Macmillan: needle through skin into lung
claims.newSentence: Another option is a CT-guided needle biopsy, in which a thin hollow needle is passed through the chest wall into the lung.

claims.sentence: The radiologist asks the person to hold their breath while a fine needle goes through the skin into the lung.
claims.evidence: Not carried; breath-holding appeared only in a trial protocol about the X-ray

claims.sentence: Pressure may be felt during sampling, and a chest X-ray usually follows an hour or more later to check the lung.

claims.newSentence: A chest X-ray afterwards is the standard way to check for a collapsed lung (pneumothorax), which is a known risk of the biopsy.

claims.sentence: Other tests can include a PET-CT scan, a blood test for tumour DNA and a bone scan to check whether the cancer has spread.
claims.evidence: PET-CT and liquid biopsy (blood test for lung cancer DNA) retrieved; bone scan not retrieved
claims.newSentence: A PET-CT scan is typically used when a CT scan has shown cancer. A biopsy is usually how doctors confirm lung cancer.

claims.sentence: The NHS says surgery is the main option for lung cancer, and that chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted medicines or immunotherapy may also be used.
claims.evidence: NHS: you may be offered a combination of surgery, chemo, radiotherapy, targeted medicines; immunotherapy may also be used. 'Main option' not carried
claims.newSentence: The NHS says that you may be offered a combination of treatments, including surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and targeted medicines, and that immunotherapy may also be used.

claims.sentence: Cancer Research UK says surgery is generally for early-stage disease, and after surgery the doctor may offer treatment to lower the chance of the cancer coming back.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: NHS says surgery generally first option for NSCLC in one lung in good health, may be followed by chemotherapy; the CRUK attribution and 'lower chance of returning' not carried
claims.newSentence: For non-small cell lung cancer, the NHS says surgery is generally the first option when the cancer is in one lung and the person is in good health, and it may be followed by a course of chemotherapy.

claims.sentence: Radiotherapy is often used on its own, but it may also be given together with or after chemotherapy or surgery.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: radiotherapy can be used alone instead of surgery for early-stage NSCLC; combined with chemotherapy; 'after surgery' not carried
claims.newSentence: Cancer Research UK says radiotherapy can be used on its own, instead of surgery, for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer, and that it can also be combined with chemotherapy.

claims.sentence: Small cell lung cancer is usually treated with chemotherapy, on its own or with radiotherapy.
claims.evidence: NHS: usually chemotherapy alone or with radiotherapy; surgery not usually used

claims.sentence: Targeted drugs are used when a tumour has a specific genetic change, so tumour samples are sent for genetic testing to look for targets.

claims.newSentence: Targeted medicines are used when a specific molecular target is found in the tumour, so cancer cells are tested to see whether a targeted drug may suit.

claims.sentence: NHS 111 Wales notes that targeted therapies cannot cure lung cancer but can slow its spread.

claims.sentence: The NHS says targeted medicines or immunotherapy are sometimes used for advanced lung cancer that has spread to other parts of the body.

claims.sentence: Roy Castle says courses of immunotherapy often have a time limit, as long as the cancer keeps responding and there are no troublesome side effects.
claims.evidence: Not carried; retrieval showed only trial protocols (about 2 years) and forum posts

claims.sentence: Cancer Research UK says tiredness can come on during treatment, tends to get worse as treatment goes on, and can last for some weeks afterwards.

claims.sentence: Resting while also doing some gentle physical activity can help.

claims.sentence: Cancer Research UK suggests that sharing worries can make them seem less overwhelming, and that many people find counselling helpful.

notes: Search tool returns summarised text, often patent documents for type-specific claims; sentences resting only on patent text were treated as unsupported. Roy Castle types page, CRUK needle-biopsy page, CRUK coping page, Christie, St George's and Leeds pages were not returned verbatim, so first-pass claims relying on them were cut or re-sourced. CRUK/NHS attribution of several reworded sentences rests on the search summary naming the returned page (e.g. targeted-therapy 'cannot cure' sentence attributed to 111 Wales; NSCLC treatment order attributed to NHS). Pneumothorax sentence rests on a PMC article (PMC12295871). Flagged: 'stage 4 is not curable' (Roy Castle, sourced, general); survival statistics (pembrolizumab 30 vs 14 months) retrieved but deliberately not used. Final article removed the tiredness/gentle-exercise advice and immunotherapy time-limit claim. Final text counts: 3 textbook sentences of about 60.
